chunks: Ali ibn Hatim from Ahmad ibn Ali, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi al-Subhan narrated to me from Muhammad ibn Sulayman, who said: Indeed, a number of our companions gathered upon this hadith, among them Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abd Allah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and Sabbah al-Hadhdha' from Ishaq ibn Ammar from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), and Sama'ah ibn Mihran from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). Muhammad ibn Sulayman said: And I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about this hadith, and he informed me of it.

He said: 'All of these asked about the prayer in the month of Ramadan, how it is and what the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did. They all said: When the first night of Ramadan entered, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) prayed Maghrib, then prayed four rak'ahs which he used to pray after Maghrib every night, then prayed eight rak'ahs. When he prayed the final Isha and the two rak'ahs which he used to pray after the final Isha while sitting every night, he stood up and prayed twelve rak'ahs. Then he entered his house. When the people saw this and looked at the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) who had increased in prayer when Ramadan entered, they asked him about that, and he informed them: "I prayed this prayer for the virtue of the month of Ramadan over the other months."'

When it was night, he stood to pray and the people lined up behind him. He turned to them and said: 'O people, this prayer is a supererogatory (nafl) prayer, and congregation is not established for nafl. Let each man from you pray alone, and let him recite what Allah taught him from His Book. And know that there is no congregation in nafl.' So the people dispersed, and each one of them prayed on his own for himself.

When it was the night of the nineteenth of Ramadan, he bathed when the sun set and prayed Maghrib with his bath. When he prayed Maghrib and the four rak'ahs which he used to pray in the past every night after Maghrib, he entered his house. When Bilal called for the final Isha prayer, the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) came out and prayed with the people. When he finished, he prayed the two rak'ahs while sitting as he used to do every night. Then he stood up and prayed one hundred rak'ahs, reciting the Opening of the Book and 'Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad' ten times in each rak'ah. When he finished from that, he prayed his prayer which he used to pray every night in the last part of the night and offered Witr.

When it was the night of the twentieth of Ramadan, he did as he used to do before that from the nights in Ramadan: eight rak'ahs after Maghrib and twelve rak'ahs after the final Isha. When it was the night of the twenty-first, he bathed when the sun set and prayed in it as he had done on the night of the nineteenth.

When it was in the night of the twenty-two, he increased in his prayer, praying eight rak'ahs after Maghrib and twenty-two rak'ahs after the final Isha. When it was the night of the twenty-third, he bathed also as he bathed on the night of the nineteenth and as he bathed on the night of the twenty-first, then he did the same.

They said: So they asked him about the prayer of fifty, what is its status in the month of Ramadan? He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) used to pray this prayer and pray the prayer of fifty in the manner he used to pray in non-Ramadan months, and he did not decrease anything from it.'

key_terms.قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ: Say, He is Allah, the One (Surah Al-Ikhlas)

ai.seo_question: What was the Prophet's specific prayer routine and number of rak'ahs during the nights of Ramadan according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* provides a detailed chronological account of the Prophet’s (peace be upon him) voluntary prayer routine during the latter nights of Ramadan, emphasizing that these additional rak'ahs are supererogatory (nafl) rather than obligatory. It records the Prophet’s instruction to the companions to pray individually rather than in congregation, a nuance significant in Shia jurisprudence regarding the nature of Tarawih prayers. The narration also clarifies that the 'prayer of fifty' refers to the cumulative count of these specific voluntary units, which the Prophet maintained consistently alongside his regular nightly prayers.
